name: Jsonifier
workload: Read/write throughput on small typed JSON payloads (double, uint64, int64, bool, string arrays), all libraries doing UTF-8 validation, measured by an adaptive-sampling benchmark harness (BenchmarkSuite) pinned to specific commits
claimed_speedup: Double Test Read: 1345.06 MB/s vs simdjson 270.87 MB/s (~5.0x); Bool Test Read: 3090.41 MB/s vs simdjson 225.22 MB/s (~13.7x); String Test Read: 3881.15 MB/s vs simdjson 1591.5 MB/s (~2.4x); Uint64 Test Read: 2221.44 MB/s vs simdjson 637.97 MB/s (~3.5x) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: Clang 24.0.0 on Linux 6.18.40.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2; Jsonifier built with its AVX2 backend
tradeoffs: Requires C++20; compile-time reflection via member-pointer registration (no macros/codegen); ARM SVE2 backend explicitly marked experimental with known incorrect cases; NEON recommended for production ARM
caveats: Benchmark is run and published by the same author group in a companion repo (Json-Performance), not an independent third party; pinned to specific Jsonifier/Glaze/simdjson commits dated 2026-09-23, so results may shift with later commits
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "json" "fastest" language:C++ --sort stars --limit 30

name: zzzJSON
workload: Parse+stringify wall time (ms) over nativejson-benchmark-style corpora (no-number JSON, JSON from Taobao, all-JSON-combined, random short/long JSON), run via the repo's build.sh
claimed_speedup: 'All JSON Above' total time 166ms (zzzjson) vs 220ms (RapidJSON) (~1.33x); Random Short JSON 38ms vs 56ms (~1.47x); Random Long JSON 29ms vs 45ms (~1.55x); No-Number JSON 149ms vs 224ms (~1.50x) (derived from page data)
stars_or_usage: 155 stars; described in README as used at scale inside Tencent
tradeoffs: Pure C, single header, 'parse on use' lazy number handling; no SIMD, so it does not compete with simdjson/yyjson-class parsers, only with DOM libraries like RapidJSON/nlohmann/cJSON
caveats: Numbers are from 2018-era hardware and an old compiler (GCC 7.3); repository has had no commits since 2020-12-26; LICENSE file is an informal public-domain-style dedication ('do whatever you want with it'), not a recognized SPDX id, and grants no patent rights
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "json" "fastest" language:C++ --sort stars --limit 30

name: LJSON
workload: File read+parse+print+write of nativejson-benchmark-style JSON test files across LJSON's DOM/SAX/file-stream modes, on ARM64 dev board and two x86_64 PCs, -O2 builds
claimed_speedup: 'LJSON parses 131% faster and prints 147% faster than RapidJSON (with file reading and writing)' on ARM CortexA53; 'parses 75% faster and prints 133% faster' on Intel i7-10700; 'parses 166% faster and prints 215% faster' (without file I/O) on Intel i7-1260P (verbatim from README)
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O2 (per README's stated 'O2 optimization level and default option compilation')
hardware: ARM64 dev board / ARM CortexA53 (Linux-5.15); Intel i7-10700 (Ubuntu 18.04, VirtualBox); Intel i7-1260P (Debian 13, VMWare)
tradeoffs: cJSON-inspired C API; DOM/SAX dual mode with memory-pool reuse and zero-heap-allocation mode; custom ldouble float<->string codec is not fully IEEE-754 compliant (17-digit precision only) in exchange for speed
caveats: First-party benchmark run and charted by the sole author across three of their own machines, not independently reproduced; author notes numbers shift release-to-release as features are added

name: Sonic
workload: Generic and struct-binding encode/decode of a 13KB/300+key/6-layer JSON document, single-threaded and parallel Go benchmarks, plus small (400B) and large (635KB Twitter) payload variants
claimed_speedup: BenchmarkEncoder_Generic_Sonic 32393 ns/op vs StdLib 106322 ns/op (~3.3x); BenchmarkDecoder_Generic_Sonic 66812 ns/op vs StdLib 124260 ns/op (~1.9x); BenchmarkEncoder_Parallel_Binding_Sonic_Fast 10785.23 MB/s vs StdLib 3486.49 MB/s (~3.1x) (derived from page data)
tradeoffs: JIT + SIMD based, so has extra startup/warm-up and binary-size overhead; amd64/arm64 only; HTML-escaping and key-sort defaults differ from encoding/json
caveats: README benchmark uses an older Go toolchain (1.17.1) on one Mac laptop; independently corroborated on different hardware and Go 1.27+ by the third-party 'tegridy-benchie' shootout (https://github.com/mihailnica10/tegridy-benchie/blob/main/RESULTS.md), which shows a smaller but consistent ~2.0x win over encoding/json on a real 39.9MB SEC-filings JSON workload
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "sonic" bytedance json --limit 5

name: jiter
workload: Parsing 5 real SEC company-facts JSON files (39.9 MB total, 285,469 fact records) into a value/DOM and reducing to fact rows, jiter vs serde_json, at 1/2/4/8 threads, in the independent 'tegridy-benchie' shootout
claimed_speedup: 209.4 MB/s vs serde_json 104.3 MB/s at 8 threads (~2.01x); 91.9 MB/s vs serde_json 48.0 MB/s at 1 thread (~1.91x) (derived from page data)
tradeoffs: The low-level Jiter iterator API requires knowing the schema ahead of time to get its full speed; the JsonValue DOM path is the one benchmarked here; also ships a PythonParse mode aimed specifically at CPython interop
caveats: jiter's own README also publishes a Criterion micro-benchmark table (up to ~6x vs serde_json::Value on numeric workloads via CodSpeed CI) but does not state the CPU model or compiler flags, so that table alone would only support Tier C; the number reported here instead comes from the independent third-party 'tegridy-benchie' real-workload shootout, which states hardware and build flags
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/mihailnica10/tegridy-benchie/contents/RESULTS.md (repo surfaced via gh search repos "json" "benchmark" language:C++ --sort updated)

name: go-json
workload: Same real-workload SEC company-facts JSON parse+reduce benchmark (39.9MB, 285,469 records) as above, at 1/2/4/8 threads, in the independent 'tegridy-benchie' shootout
claimed_speedup: 256.7 MB/s vs encoding/json 128.8 MB/s at 8 threads (~1.99x); 90.8 MB/s vs encoding/json 44.5 MB/s at 1 thread (~2.04x) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: go 1.27+, default build flags (per repo's README.benchmark.md)
tradeoffs: Advertised and used as a full drop-in replacement for encoding/json (single import swap)
caveats: go-json's own README shows benchmark results only as chart images with no CPU/compiler stated in text, so on its own that evidence would be Tier C/D; the Tier-A number reported here comes from the independent third-party 'tegridy-benchie' shootout instead

name: simd-json (Rust)
workload: Same real-workload SEC company-facts JSON parse+reduce benchmark (39.9MB, 285,469 records) as above, at 1/2/4/8 threads, in the independent 'tegridy-benchie' shootout
claimed_speedup: 115.2 MB/s vs serde_json 104.3 MB/s at 8 threads (~1.10x); 50.6 MB/s vs serde_json 48.0 MB/s at 1 thread (~1.05x) (derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Uses substantial unsafe code for SIMD intrinsics; Rust port of simdjson's design but its own README states it does not fully reach the C++ implementation's performance; jiter beat it head-to-head in the same shootout
caveats: Margin over serde_json in this real-workload benchmark is small (~5-10%), much smaller than simdjson's own margin over RapidJSON/nlohmann in C++; the project's own README makes only a qualitative 'as close as possible to the C++ implementation' claim with no numbers at all

name: easyjson
workload: Marshal/unmarshal of a 13KB Twitter-search-style JSON document (9KB minified), an 80-byte small-request case, and a ~500KB large-request case (50 concatenated samples), using easyjson's codegen'd marshalers
claimed_speedup: 'easyjson is roughly 5-6 times faster than the standard encoding/json for unmarshaling, and 3-4 times faster for non-concurrent marshaling. Concurrent marshaling is 6-7x faster if marshaling to a writer' (verbatim from README)
tradeoffs: Requires an ahead-of-time codegen step (easyjson -all file.go), so it is not a drop-in import swap like go-json/sonic; default fast path uses unsafe
caveats: No CPU model, Go version, or compiler flags stated anywhere in the README; the speedups are given as rounded 'roughly N-Mx' ranges rather than exact benchmark output
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/mailru/easyjson (cross-referenced from goccy/go-json's library-comparison table)

name: jsoniter (json-iterator/go)
workload: Same real-workload SEC company-facts JSON parse+reduce benchmark (39.9MB, 285,469 records) as above, at 1/2/4/8 threads, in the independent 'tegridy-benchie' shootout
claimed_speedup: 233.6 MB/s vs encoding/json 128.8 MB/s at 8 threads (~1.81x); 79.3 MB/s vs encoding/json 44.5 MB/s at 1 thread (~1.78x) (derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Advertised as a '100% compatible drop-in replacement' for encoding/json, but goccy/go-json's README documents real compatibility gaps in that claim
caveats: Repository is archived by its owner and no longer maintained; the performance figure here comes from an independent third-party shootout rather than the project's own (now-stale) historical benchmark claims
